excerpt.html: The typical <mark>test objectives</mark> are:
Causing <mark>failures</mark> and finding <mark>defects</mark>
Ensuring required <mark>coverage</mark> of a <mark>test object</mark>
Reducing the <mark>risk</mark> level of inadequate software <mark>quality</mark>
Verifying that a <mark>test object</mark> complies with contractual, legal, and regulatory requirements
Building confidence in the <mark>quality</mark> of the <mark>test object</mark>
Validating whether the <mark>test object</mark> is complete and works as expected by the stakeholders

<mark>Test objectives</mark> can vary, depending upon the context, which includes the work product being tested, the test level, <mark>risks</mark>, the software development lifecycle (SDLC) being followed, and factors related to the business context, e.g., corporate structure, competitive considerations, or time to market.

Testing and <mark>debugging</mark> are separate activities. … Testing can trigger <mark>failures</mark> that are caused by <mark>defects</mark> in the software (<mark>dynamic testing</mark>) or can directly find <mark>defects</mark> in the <mark>test object</mark> (<mark>static testing</mark>). … When <mark>dynamic testing</mark> (see chapter 4) triggers a <mark>failure</mark>, <mark>debugging</mark> is concerned with finding causes of this <mark>failure</mark> (<mark>defects</mark>), analyzing these causes, and eliminating them. … The typical <mark>debugging</mark> process in this case involves:
Reproduction of a <mark>failure</mark>
Diagnosis (finding the <mark>defect</mark>)
Fixing the <mark>defect</mark>

Subsequent <mark>confirmation testing</mark> checks whether the fixes resolved the problem. … Preferably, <mark>confirmation testing</mark> is done by the same person who performed the initial test. … Subsequent regression testing can also be performed, to check whether the fixes are causing <mark>failures</mark> in other parts of the <mark>test object</mark> (see section 2.2.3 for more information on <mark>confirmation testing</mark> and regression testing). … When <mark>static testing</mark> identifies a <mark>defect</mark>, <mark>debugging</mark> is concerned with removing it. … There is no need for reproduction or diagnosis, since <mark>static testing</mark> directly finds <mark>defects</mark>, and cannot cause <mark>failures</mark> (see chapter 3).

efd.statement: Recall the relation between testing and <mark>quality</mark> assurance

excerpt.html: While people often use the terms “testing” and “<mark>quality</mark> assurance” (QA) interchangeably, testing and QA are not the same. … Testing is a product-oriented, corrective approach that focuses on those activities supporting the achievement of appropriate levels of <mark>quality</mark>. … Testing is a major form of <mark>quality</mark> control, while others include formal methods (model checking and proof of correctness), simulation and prototyping. … In testing they are used to fix <mark>defects</mark>, while in QA they provide feedback on how well the development and test processes are performing.

efd.section: 1.2.3 Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes

excerpt.html: Human beings make <mark>errors</mark> (mistakes), which produce <mark>defects</mark> (faults, bugs), which in turn may result in <mark>failures</mark>. … Humans make <mark>errors</mark> for various reasons, such as time pressure, complexity of work products, processes, infrastructure or interactions, or simply because they are tired or lack adequate training. … <mark>Defects</mark> can be found in documentation, such as a requirements specification or a test script, in source code, or in a supporting work product such as a build file. … <mark>Defects</mark> in work products produced earlier in the SDLC, if undetected, often lead to defective work products later in the lifecycle. … If a <mark>defect</mark> in code is executed, the system may fail to do what it should do, or do something it shouldn’t, causing a <mark>failure</mark>. … Some <mark>defects</mark> will always result in a <mark>failure</mark> if executed, while others will only result in a <mark>failure</mark> in specific circumstances, and some may never result in a <mark>failure</mark>. … <mark>Errors</mark> and <mark>defects</mark> are not the only cause of <mark>failures</mark>. … <mark>Failures</mark> can also be caused by environmental conditions, such as when radiation or electromagnetic fields cause <mark>defects</mark> in firmware. … A <mark>root cause</mark> is a fundamental reason for the occurrence of a problem (e.g., a situation that leads to an <mark>error</mark>). … <mark>Root causes</mark> are identified through <mark>root cause</mark> analysis, which is typically performed when a <mark>failure</mark> occurs or a <mark>defect</mark> is identified. … It is believed that further similar <mark>failures</mark> or <mark>defects</mark> can be prevented or their frequency reduced by addressing the <mark>root cause</mark>, such as by removing it.

… Testing shows the presence, not the absence of <mark>defects</mark>. … Testing can show that <mark>defects</mark> are present in the test object, but cannot prove that there are no <mark>defects</mark> (Buxton 1970). … Testing reduces the probability of <mark>defects</mark> remaining undiscovered in the test object, but even if no <mark>defects</mark> are found, testing cannot prove test object correctness.

… <mark>Exhaustive testing is impossible</mark>. … Rather than attempting to test exhaustively, test techniques (see chapter 4), <mark>test case</mark> prioritization (see section 5.1.5), and risk-based testing (see section 5.2), should be used to focus test efforts.

… <mark>Defects</mark> that are removed early in the process will not cause subsequent <mark>defects</mark> in derived work products. … The cost of quality will be reduced since fewer <mark>failures</mark> will occur later in the SDLC (Boehm 1981). … To find <mark>defects</mark> early, both static testing (see chapter 3) and dynamic testing (see chapter 4) should be started as early as possible.

… <mark>Defects</mark> cluster together. … A small number of system components usually contain most of the <mark>defects</mark> discovered or are responsible for most of the operational <mark>failures</mark> (Enders 1975). … Predicted <mark>defect</mark> clusters, and actual <mark>defect</mark> clusters observed during testing or in operation, are an important input for risk-based testing (see section 5.2).
… If the same tests are repeated many times, they become increasingly ineffective in detecting new <mark>defects</mark> (Beizer 1990). …
… Testing is <mark>context dependent</mark>. …

… Thoroughly testing all the specified requirements and fixing all the <mark>defects</mark> found could still produce a system that does not fulfill the users’ needs and expectations, that does not help in achieving the customer’s business goals, and that is inferior compared to other competing systems. … In addition to verification, <mark>validation</mark> should also be carried out (Boehm 1981).

… While testing involves <mark>verification</mark>, i.e., checking whether the system meets specified requirements, it also involves <mark>validation</mark>, which means checking whether the system meets users’ and other stakeholders’ needs in its operational environment. … Static testing includes <mark>reviews</mark> (see chapter 3) and static analysis. …

activities.statement: Explain the different test <mark>activities</mark> and related tasks

excerpt.html: A <mark>test process</mark> usually consists of the main groups of <mark>activities</mark> described below. … Although many of these <mark>activities</mark> may appear to follow a logical sequence, they are often implemented iteratively or in parallel. … These testing <mark>activities</mark> usually need to be tailored to the system and the project. … <mark>Test planning</mark> consists of defining the <mark>test objectives</mark> and then selecting an approach that best achieves the objectives within the constraints imposed by the overall context. … <mark>Test planning</mark> is further explained in section 5.1.

<mark>Test monitoring</mark> and test <mark>control</mark>. … <mark>Test monitoring</mark> involves the ongoing checking of all test <mark>activities</mark> and the comparison of actual progress against the plan. … Test <mark>control</mark> involves taking the actions necessary to meet the <mark>test objectives</mark>. … <mark>Test monitoring</mark> and test <mark>control</mark> are further explained in section 5.3. … <mark>Test analysis</mark> includes analyzing the <mark>test basis</mark> to identify testable features. … Associated <mark>test conditions</mark> are defined and prioritized, taking the related <mark>risks</mark> and <mark>risk</mark> levels into account (see section 5.2). … The <mark>test basis</mark> and the <mark>test object</mark> are also evaluated to identify <mark>defects</mark> they may contain and to assess their testability. … <mark>Test analysis</mark> is often supported by the use of <mark>test techniques</mark> (see chapter 4). … <mark>Test analysis</mark> answers the question “what to test?” in terms of measurable <mark>coverage</mark> criteria. … <mark>Test design</mark> includes elaborating the <mark>test conditions</mark> into <mark>test cases</mark> and other <mark>testware</mark> (e.g., <mark>test charters</mark>). … This activity often involves the identification of <mark>coverage items</mark>, which serve as a guide to specify <mark>test case</mark> inputs. … <mark>Test techniques</mark> (see chapter 4) can be used to support this activity. … <mark>Test design</mark> also includes defining the <mark>test data requirements</mark>, designing the test environment and identifying the necessary infrastructure and tools. … <mark>Test design</mark> answers the question “how to test?”. … <mark>Test implementation</mark> includes creating or acquiring the <mark>testware</mark> necessary for <mark>test execution</mark> (e.g., <mark>test data</mark>). … <mark>Test cases</mark> can be organized into <mark>test procedures</mark>, which are often assembled into <mark>test suites</mark>. … <mark>Test procedures</mark> are prioritized and arranged within a <mark>test execution schedule</mark> for efficient <mark>test execution</mark> (see section 5.1.5). … The test environment is built and verified to be <mark>set up</mark> correctly. … <mark>Test execution</mark> includes running the tests in accordance with the <mark>test execution schedule</mark> (test runs). … <mark>Test execution</mark> may be manual or automated. … <mark>Test execution</mark> can take many forms, including continuous testing or pair testing sessions. … This <mark>analysis</mark> allows us to <mark>report</mark> the anomalies based on the failures observed (see section 5.5). … <mark>Test completion</mark> usually occurs at project milestones (e.g., <mark>release</mark>, <mark>end of iteration</mark>, <mark>test level</mark> <mark>completion</mark>). … For any unresolved <mark>defects</mark>, <mark>change requests</mark> or <mark>product backlog items</mark> are created. … Any <mark>testware</mark> that may be useful in the future is identified and archived or handed over to the appropriate teams. … The test <mark>activities</mark> are analyzed to identify <mark>lessons learned</mark> and improvements for future iterations, <mark>releases</mark>, or projects (see section 2.1.6). … A <mark>test completion report</mark> is created and communicated to the <mark>stakeholders</mark>.

activities.statement: Explain the impact of context on the test process

excerpt.html: … Test <mark>activities</mark> are an integral part of the development processes carried out within an organization. … Testing is also funded by <mark>stakeholders</mark> and its final goal is to help fulfill the <mark>stakeholders</mark>’ business needs. …
<mark>Stakeholders</mark> (needs, expectations, requirements, willingness to cooperate, etc.)
Business domain (criticality of the <mark>test object</mark>, identified <mark>risks</mark>, market needs, specific legal <mark>regulations</mark>, etc.)
Project constraints (scope, time, budget, <mark>resources</mark>, etc.)

These factors will have an impact on many test-related issues, including: test <mark>strategy</mark>, <mark>test techniques</mark> used, degree of test automation, required level of <mark>coverage</mark>, level of detail of <mark>testware</mark>, test <mark>reporting</mark>, etc.

activities.statement: Compare the different roles in testing

excerpt.html: In this syllabus, two principal roles in testing are covered: a test <mark>management</mark> role and a testing role. … The <mark>activities</mark> and tasks assigned to these two roles depend on factors such as the project and product context, the skills of the people in the roles, and the organization. … The test <mark>management</mark> role takes overall responsibility for the <mark>test process</mark>, test team and leadership of the test <mark>activities</mark>. … The test <mark>management</mark> role is mainly focused on the <mark>activities</mark> of <mark>test planning</mark>, <mark>test monitoring</mark>, test <mark>control</mark> and <mark>test completion</mark>. … The way in which the test <mark>management</mark> role is carried out varies depending on the context. … For example, in Agile software development, some of the test <mark>management</mark> tasks may be handled by the Agile team. … Tasks that span multiple teams or the entire organization may be performed by <mark>test managers</mark> outside of the development team. … The testing role is mainly focused on the <mark>activities</mark> of <mark>test analysis</mark>, <mark>test design</mark>, <mark>test implementation</mark> and <mark>test execution</mark>. … For example, the test <mark>management</mark> role can be performed by a team leader, by a <mark>test manager</mark>, by a development manager, etc. … It is also possible for one person to take on the roles of testing and test <mark>management</mark> at the same time.

testware.statement: Differentiate the <mark>testware</mark> that supports the test activities

excerpt.html: <mark>Testware</mark> is created as <mark>output</mark> work products from the test activities described in section 1.4.1. …

Test <mark>planning</mark> work products include: test plan, test schedule, risk register, entry criteria and <mark>exit criteria</mark> (see section 5.1). Risk register is a list of risks together with risk likelihood, risk impact and information about risk mitigation (see section 5.2). Test schedule, risk register, entry criteria and <mark>exit criteria</mark> are often a part of the test plan.

Test monitoring and test control work products include: test <mark>progress reports</mark> (see section 5.3.2), documentation of control directives (see section 5.3) and information about risks (see section 5.2).

Test analysis work products include: (prioritized) <mark>test conditions</mark> (e.g., acceptance criteria, see section 4.5.2), and <mark>defect reports</mark> regarding <mark>defects</mark> in the <mark>test basis</mark> (if not fixed directly).
Test design work products include: (prioritized) <mark>test cases</mark>, test charters, <mark>coverage</mark> items, <mark>test data</mark> requirements and test environment requirements.

Test implementation work products include: test procedures, manual and automated test scripts, test suites, <mark>test data</mark>, test <mark>execution</mark> schedule, and test environment items. Examples of test environment items include: stubs, drivers, simulators, and service virtualizations.
Test <mark>execution</mark> work products include: test logs, and <mark>defect reports</mark> (see section 5.5).

Test <mark>completion</mark> work products include: test <mark>completion report</mark> (see section 5.3.2), <mark>action items</mark> for improvement of subsequent projects or iterations, documented <mark>lessons learned</mark>, and <mark>change requests</mark> (e.g., as product backlog items).

testware.section: 1.4.4 Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware

excerpt.html: To implement effective test monitoring and test control, it is important to establish and maintain <mark>traceability</mark> throughout the test process between the <mark>test basis</mark> elements, <mark>testware</mark> associated with these elements (e.g., <mark>test conditions</mark>, risks, <mark>test cases</mark>), <mark>test results</mark>, and <mark>defects</mark>. … Accurate <mark>traceability</mark> supports <mark>coverage</mark> evaluation, so it is very useful if measurable <mark>coverage</mark> criteria are defined in the <mark>test basis</mark>. … The <mark>coverage</mark> criteria can function as key performance indicators to drive the activities that show to what extent the test objectives have been achieved (see section 1.1.1). …
<mark>Traceability</mark> of <mark>test cases</mark> to requirements can verify that the requirements are covered by <mark>test cases</mark>.
<mark>Traceability</mark> of <mark>test results</mark> to risks can be used to evaluate the level of residual risk in a test object.

In addition to evaluating <mark>coverage</mark>, good <mark>traceability</mark> makes it possible to determine the impact of changes, facilitates audits, and helps meet IT governance criteria. … Good <mark>traceability</mark> also makes test <mark>progress reports</mark> and test <mark>completion reports</mark> more easily understandable by including the status of <mark>test basis</mark> elements. … <mark>Traceability</mark> provides information to assess product quality, process capability, and project progress against business goals.

independence.statement: Distinguish the benefits and drawbacks of <mark>independence</mark> of testing

excerpt.html: A certain degree of <mark>independence</mark> makes the tester more effective at finding <mark>defects</mark> due to differences between the author’s and the tester’s <mark>cognitive biases</mark> (cf. … <mark>Independence</mark> is not, however, a replacement for familiarity, e.g., developers can efficiently find many <mark>defects</mark> in their own code. … Work products can be tested by their author (no <mark>independence</mark>), by the author's peers from the same team (some <mark>independence</mark>), by testers from outside the author's team but within the organization (high <mark>independence</mark>), or by testers from outside the organization (<mark>very high</mark> <mark>independence</mark>). … For most projects, it is usually best to carry out testing with multiple levels of <mark>independence</mark> (e.g., developers performing component testing and component integration testing, test team performing system and system integration testing, and business representatives performing acceptance testing).

The main benefit of <mark>independence</mark> of testing is that independent testers are likely to recognize different kinds of <mark>failures</mark> and <mark>defects</mark> compared to developers because of their different backgrounds, technical perspectives, and biases. … Independent testers may be <mark>isolated from the development team</mark>, which may lead to a lack of collaboration, communication problems, or an <mark>adversarial relationship</mark> with the development team. … Developers may lose a sense of responsibility for <mark>quality</mark>. …

wholeteam.statement: Give examples of the generic skills required for testing

excerpt.html: While being generic, the following skills are particularly relevant for testers:
<mark>Testing knowledge</mark> (to increase effectiveness of testing, e.g., by using test techniques)
Thoroughness, carefulness, <mark>curiosity</mark>, <mark>attention to details</mark>, being methodical (to identify <mark>defects</mark>, especially the ones that are difficult to find)

Good <mark>communication</mark> skills, active listening, being a <mark>team player</mark> (to interact effectively with all stakeholders, to convey information to others, to be understood, and to report and discuss <mark>defects</mark>)
Analytical thinking, <mark>critical thinking</mark>, <mark>creativity</mark> (to increase effectiveness of testing)
<mark>Technical knowledge</mark> (to increase efficiency of testing, e.g., by using appropriate test tools)
<mark>Domain knowledge</mark> (to be able to understand and to communicate with end users/business representatives)

… This makes <mark>communication</mark> skills crucial for testers. … Some people may perceive testing as a destructive activity, even though it contributes greatly to project success and product <mark>quality</mark>. … To try to improve this view, information about <mark>defects</mark> and failures should be communicated in a constructive way.

wholeteam.statement: Recall the advantages of the <mark>whole</mark> team approach

excerpt.html: … The <mark>whole</mark> team approach – a practice coming from Extreme Programming (see section 2.1) – builds upon this skill. … In the <mark>whole</mark> team approach any team member with the necessary knowledge and skills can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for <mark>quality</mark>. … The team members share the same workspace (physical or virtual), as co-location facilitates <mark>communication</mark> and interaction. … The <mark>whole</mark> team approach improves team dynamics, enhances <mark>communication</mark> and collaboration within the team, and creates synergy by allowing the various skill sets within the team to be leveraged for the benefit of the project. … Testers work closely with other team members to ensure that the desired <mark>quality</mark> levels are achieved. … This includes collaborating with business representatives to help them create suitable acceptance tests and working with developers to agree on the test strategy and decide on <mark>test automation</mark> approaches. … Testers can thus transfer <mark>testing knowledge</mark> to other team members and influence the development of the product. … Depending on the context, the <mark>whole</mark> team approach may not always be appropriate. …

sdlc.statement: Explain the impact of the chosen software development lifecycle on testing
sdlc.section: 2.1.1 Impact of the Software Development Lifecycle on Testing
keywords: scope and timing of test activities

excerpt.html: Testing must be adapted to the SDLC to succeed. The choice of the SDLC impacts on the:
<mark>Scope and timing of test activities</mark> (e.g., <mark>test levels</mark> and test types)
Choice of <mark>test techniques</mark> and <mark>test approach</mark>
<mark>Extent of test automation</mark>

In <mark>sequential development models</mark>, in the initial phases testers typically participate in requirement <mark>reviews</mark>, <mark>test analysis</mark>, and test design. … In some <mark>iterative development models</mark> and <mark>incremental development models</mark>, it is assumed that each iteration delivers a working prototype or product increment. … This implies that in each iteration both static testing and dynamic testing may be performed at all <mark>test levels</mark>. … Frequent delivery of increments requires fast feedback and extensive <mark>regression testing</mark>. … <mark>Agile software development</mark> assumes that change may occur throughout the project. … Therefore, lightweight work product documentation and extensive <mark>test automation</mark> to make <mark>regression testing</mark> easier are favored in agile projects. … Also, most of the manual testing tends to be done using experience-based <mark>test techniques</mark> (see Section 4.4) that do not require extensive prior <mark>test analysis</mark> and design.

sdlc.statement: Recall good testing practices that apply to all software development lifecycles
sdlc.section: 2.1.2 Software Development Lifecycle and Good Testing Practices

excerpt.html: Good testing practices, independent of the chosen SDLC model, include the following:
Different <mark>test levels</mark> (see chapter 2.2.1) have specific and different <mark>test objectives</mark>, which allows for testing to be appropriately comprehensive while avoiding redundancy

<mark>Test analysis</mark> and design for a given <mark>test level</mark> begins during the corresponding development phase of the SDLC, so that testing can adhere to the principle of early testing (see section 1.3)
In this syllabus, the following five <mark>test levels</mark> are described:

<mark>Component testing</mark> (also known as unit testing) focuses on testing <mark>components</mark> in isolation. It often requires specific support, such as test harnesses or <mark>unit test frameworks</mark>. <mark>Component testing</mark> is normally <mark>performed by developers</mark> in their development environments.

<mark>Component integration testing</mark> (also known as unit <mark>integration testing</mark>) focuses on testing the <mark>interfaces and interactions between components</mark>. <mark>Component integration testing</mark> is heavily dependent on the integration strategy like <mark>bottom-up</mark>, <mark>top-down</mark> or <mark>big-bang</mark>.

<mark>System testing</mark> focuses on the overall behavior and capabilities of an entire system or product, often including functional testing of <mark>end-to-end tasks</mark> and the non-functional testing of quality characteristics. For some non-functional quality characteristics, it is preferable to test them on a complete system in a representative test environment (e.g., usability). Using simulations of subsystems is also possible. <mark>System testing</mark> may be performed by an independent test team, and is related to specifications for the system.

<mark>System integration testing</mark> focuses on testing the interfaces of the system under test and other systems and <mark>external services</mark>. <mark>System integration testing</mark> requires suitable test environments preferably similar to the operational environment.

<mark>Acceptance testing</mark> focuses on <mark>validation</mark> and on demonstrating readiness for deployment, which means that the system fulfills the user’s business needs. Ideally, <mark>acceptance testing</mark> should be performed by the intended users. The main forms of <mark>acceptance testing</mark> are: user <mark>acceptance testing</mark> (UAT), operational <mark>acceptance testing</mark>, contractual <mark>acceptance testing</mark> and regulatory <mark>acceptance testing</mark>, alpha testing and beta testing.
<mark>Test levels</mark> are distinguished by the following non-exhaustive list of attributes, to avoid overlapping of test activities:
<mark>Test object</mark>

A lot of <mark>test types</mark> exist and can be applied in projects. … In this syllabus, the following four <mark>test types</mark> are addressed: <mark>Functional testing</mark> evaluates the functions that a component or system should perform. … The functions are “what” the <mark>test object</mark> should do. … The main objective of <mark>functional testing</mark> is checking the <mark>functional</mark> <mark>completeness</mark>, <mark>functional</mark> <mark>correctness</mark> and <mark>functional</mark> <mark>appropriateness</mark>. … <mark>Non-functional testing</mark> evaluates attributes other than <mark>functional</mark> characteristics of a component or system. … <mark>Non-functional testing</mark> is the testing of “<mark>how well the system behaves</mark>”. … The main objective of nonfunctional testing is checking the <mark>non-functional</mark> quality characteristics. … The ISO/IEC 25010 standard provides the following classification of the <mark>non-functional</mark> quality characteristics:
<mark>Performance efficiency</mark>
<mark>Compatibility</mark>
<mark>Usability</mark> (also known as interaction capability)
<mark>Reliability</mark>
<mark>Security</mark>
<mark>Maintainability</mark>
<mark>Portability</mark> (also known as flexibility)

It is sometimes appropriate for <mark>non-functional testing</mark> to start early in the SDLC (e.g., as part of reviews or <mark>component testing</mark>). … Many <mark>non-functional</mark> tests are derived from <mark>functional</mark> tests as they use the same <mark>functional</mark> tests, but check that while performing the function, a <mark>non-functional</mark> constraint is satisfied (e.g., checking that a function performs within a specified time, or a function can be ported to a new platform). … The late discovery of <mark>non-functional</mark> <mark>defects</mark> can pose a serious threat to the success of a project. … Nonfunctional testing sometimes needs a very specific test environment, such as a <mark>usability</mark> lab for <mark>usability</mark> testing. … <mark>Black-box testing</mark> (see section 4.2) is <mark>specification-based</mark> and derives tests from documentation not related to the internal structure of the <mark>test object</mark>. … The main objective of <mark>black-box testing</mark> is checking the system's behavior against its specifications. … <mark>White-box testing</mark> (see section 4.3) is <mark>structure-based</mark> and derives tests from the system's implementation or internal structure (e.g., code, <mark>architecture</mark>, work flows, and <mark>data flows</mark>). … The main objective of <mark>white-box testing</mark> is to cover the underlying structure by the tests to an acceptable <mark>level</mark>. … All the four above mentioned <mark>test types</mark> can be applied to all <mark>test levels</mark>, although the focus will be different at each <mark>level</mark>. … Different test techniques can be used to derive test conditions and test cases for all the mentioned <mark>test types</mark>.

Changes are typically made to a component or system to either enhance it by adding a new feature or to fix it by removing a <mark>defect</mark>. … Testing should then also include <mark>confirmation testing</mark> and <mark>regression testing</mark>. … <mark>Confirmation testing</mark> confirms that an original <mark>defect</mark> has been successfully fixed. …
executing all tests that previously have <mark>failed</mark> due to the <mark>defect</mark>, or, also by
adding new tests to cover any changes that were needed to fix the <mark>defect</mark>

However, when time or money is short when fixing <mark>defects</mark>, <mark>confirmation testing</mark> might be restricted to simply exercising the test steps that should reproduce the failure caused by the <mark>defect</mark> and checking that the failure does not occur. … <mark>Regression testing</mark> confirms that no adverse consequences have been caused by a change, including a fix that has already been <mark>confirmation</mark> tested. … <mark>Regression testing</mark> may not be restricted to the test object itself but can also be related to the environment. … It is advisable first to perform an impact analysis to recognize the extent of the <mark>regression testing</mark>. … <mark>Regression</mark> test suites are run many times and generally the number of <mark>regression</mark> <mark>test cases</mark> will increase with each iteration or release, so <mark>regression testing</mark> is a strong candidate for automation. … Where CI is used, such as in DevOps (see section 2.1.4), it is good practice to also include automated <mark>regression</mark> tests. … Depending on the situation, this may include <mark>regression</mark> tests on different test levels. … <mark>Confirmation testing</mark> and/or <mark>regression testing</mark> for the test object are needed on all test levels if <mark>defects</mark> are fixed and/or changes are made on these test levels.
… The scope of <mark>maintenance testing</mark> typically depends on:
The triggers for maintenance and <mark>maintenance testing</mark> can be classified as follows:
<mark>Modifications</mark>, such as planned enhancements (i.e., release-based), corrective changes or hot fixes.

Upgrades or <mark>migrations</mark> of the operational environment, such as from one platform to another, which can require tests associated with the new environment as well as of the changed software, or tests of data conversion when data from another application is migrated into the system being maintained.

<mark>Retirement</mark>, such as when an application reaches the end of its life. When a system is retired, this can require testing of data archiving if long data retention periods are required. Testing of restore and retrieval procedures after archiving may also be needed in the event that certain data is required during the archiving period.

testfirst.statement: Recall the examples of test-first approaches to development
testfirst.section: 2.1.3 Testing as a Driver for Software Development

excerpt.html: TDD, ATDD and BDD are similar development approaches, where tests are defined as a means of directing development. Each of these approaches implements the principle of early testing (see section 1.3) and follows shift left (see section 2.1.5), since the tests are defined before the code is written. They support an iterative development model. These approaches are characterized as follows: Test-Driven Development (TDD):
Directs the coding through <mark>test cases</mark> (instead of extensive software design) (Beck 2003)
Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD) (see section 4.5.3):
Derives tests from <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> as part of the system design process (Gärtner 2011)
Behavior-Driven Development (BDD):

Expresses the desired behavior of an application with <mark>test cases</mark> written in a simple form of natural language, which is easy to understand by stakeholders – usually using the Given/When/Then format (Chelimsky 2010)
<mark>Test cases</mark> should then automatically be translated into executable tests

The principle of early testing (see section 1.3) is sometimes referred to as <mark>shift left</mark> because it is an approach where testing is performed earlier in the SDLC. … <mark>Shift left</mark> basically suggests that testing should be done earlier (e.g., not waiting for code to be implemented or for components to be integrated), but it does not mean that testing later in the SDLC should be neglected. … There are some good practices that illustrate how to achieve a “<mark>shift left</mark>” in testing, which include:

Reviewing the specification from the perspective of testers. These <mark>review</mark> activities on specifications often find potential defects, such as ambiguities, incompleteness, and inconsistencies
Completing <mark>static analysis</mark> of source code prior to <mark>dynamic testing</mark>, or as part of an automated process

Performing non-functional testing starting at the component <mark>test level</mark>, where possible. This is a form of <mark>shift left</mark> as these non-functional test types tend to be performed later in the SDLC when a complete system and a representative test environment are available

<mark>Shift left</mark> might result in extra training, effort and/or costs earlier in the process but is expected to save efforts and/or costs later in the process. … For <mark>shift left</mark> it is important that stakeholders are convinced and bought into this concept.

shiftleft.statement: Explain how <mark>retrospectives</mark> can be used as a mechanism for process improvement

excerpt.html: <mark>Retrospectives</mark> are often held at the end of a project or an iteration, at a release milestone, or can be held when needed. … The timing and organization of the <mark>retrospectives</mark> depend on the particular SDLC model being followed. …
… <mark>Retrospectives</mark> are critical for the successful implementation of continuous improvement, and it is important that any recommended improvements are followed up. …
Increased <mark>quality</mark> of <mark>testware</mark> (e.g., by jointly reviewing the test processes)
Improved <mark>quality</mark> of the <mark>test basis</mark> (e.g., as deficiencies in the extent and <mark>quality</mark> of the requirements could be addressed and solved)

staticdyn.statement: Recognize types of work products that can be examined by <mark>static testing</mark>
staticdyn.section: 3.1.1 Work Products Examinable by Static Testing

excerpt.html: Almost any work product can be examined using <mark>static testing</mark>. … However, for <mark>static analysis</mark>, work products need a structure against which they can be checked (e.g., models, code or text with a formal syntax). … Work products that are not appropriate for <mark>static testing</mark> include those that are difficult to interpret by human beings and that should not be analyzed by tools (e.g., 3rd party executable code due to legal reasons).

staticdyn.statement: Compare and contrast <mark>static testing</mark> and <mark>dynamic testing</mark>
staticdyn.section: 3.1.3 Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing

excerpt.html: <mark>Static testing</mark> and <mark>dynamic testing</mark> practices complement each other. … They have similar objectives, such as supporting the detection of <mark>defects</mark> in work products (see section 1.1.1), but there are also some differences, such as:

<mark>Static testing</mark> and <mark>dynamic testing</mark> (with analysis of <mark>failures</mark>) can both lead to the detection of <mark>defects</mark>, however there are some <mark>defect</mark> types that can only be found by either <mark>static</mark> or <mark>dynamic testing</mark>.

<mark>Static testing</mark> finds <mark>defects</mark> directly, while <mark>dynamic testing</mark> causes <mark>failures</mark> from which the associated <mark>defects</mark> are determined through subsequent analysis
<mark>Static testing</mark> may more easily detect <mark>defects</mark> that lay on paths through the code that are rarely executed or hard to reach using <mark>dynamic testing</mark>
<mark>Static testing</mark> can be applied to non-executable work products, while <mark>dynamic testing</mark> can only be applied to executable work products

<mark>Static testing</mark> can be used to measure quality characteristics that are not dependent on executing code (e.g., maintainability), while <mark>dynamic testing</mark> can be used to measure quality characteristics that are dependent on executing code (e.g., performance efficiency)
Typical <mark>defects</mark> that are easier and/or cheaper to find through <mark>static testing</mark> include:
<mark>Defects</mark> in requirements (e.g., inconsistencies, ambiguities, contradictions, omissions, inaccuracies, duplications)
Design <mark>defects</mark> (e.g., inefficient database structures, poor modularization)

reviews.statement: Recall which responsibilities are assigned to the principal roles when performing <mark>reviews</mark>

excerpt.html: <mark>Reviews</mark> involve various stakeholders, who may take on several roles. …
<mark>Manager</mark> – decides what is to be reviewed and provides resources, such as staff and time for the <mark>review</mark>
Author – creates and fixes the work product under <mark>review</mark>

Moderator (also known as the facilitator) – ensures the effective running of <mark>review</mark> meetings, including mediation, time management, and a safe <mark>review</mark> environment in which everyone can speak freely

<mark>Scribe</mark> (also known as recorder) – collates anomalies from reviewers and records <mark>review</mark> information, such as decisions and new anomalies found during the <mark>review</mark> meeting
Reviewer – performs <mark>reviews</mark>. A reviewer may be someone working on the project, a subject matter expert, or any other stakeholder
<mark>Review leader</mark> – takes overall responsibility for the <mark>review</mark> such as deciding who will be involved, and organizing when and where the <mark>review</mark> will take place

reviews.statement: Compare and contrast the different <mark>review</mark> types

excerpt.html: There exist many <mark>review</mark> types ranging from <mark>informal reviews</mark> to formal <mark>reviews</mark>. … The same work product can be reviewed with different <mark>review</mark> types, e.g., first an informal one and later a more formal one. … Selecting the right <mark>review</mark> type is key to achieving the required <mark>review</mark> objectives (see section 3.2.5). … Some commonly used <mark>review</mark> types are:
<mark>Informal review</mark>. <mark>Informal reviews</mark> do not follow a defined process and do not require a formal documented output. The main objective is detecting anomalies.

<mark>Walkthrough</mark>. A <mark>walkthrough</mark>, which is led by the author, can serve many objectives, such as evaluating quality and building confidence in the work product, educating reviewers, gaining consensus, generating new ideas, motivating and enabling authors to improve and detecting anomalies. Reviewers might perform an individual <mark>review</mark> before the <mark>walkthrough</mark>, but this is not required.

<mark>Technical Review</mark>. A <mark>technical review</mark> is performed by technically qualified reviewers and led by a moderator. The objectives of a <mark>technical review</mark> are to gain consensus and make decisions regarding a technical problem, but also to detect anomalies, evaluate quality and build confidence in the work product, generate new ideas, and to motivate and enable authors to improve.

<mark>Inspection</mark>. As <mark>inspections</mark> are the most formal type of <mark>review</mark>, they follow the complete generic process (see section 3.2.2). The main objective is to find the maximum number of anomalies. Other objectives are to evaluate quality, build confidence in the work product, and to motivate and enable authors to improve. Metrics are collected and used to improve the SDLC, including the <mark>inspection</mark> process. In <mark>inspections</mark>, the author cannot act as the <mark>review leader</mark> or <mark>scribe</mark>.

success.statement: Recall the <mark>factors</mark> that contribute to a successful <mark>review</mark>

excerpt.html: There are several <mark>factors</mark> that determine the <mark>success</mark> of <mark>reviews</mark>, which include:
Defining clear objectives and measurable <mark>exit criteria</mark>. Evaluation of participants should never be an objective
Choosing the appropriate <mark>review</mark> type to achieve the given objectives, and to suit the type of work product, the <mark>review</mark> participants, the project needs and context
Performing <mark>reviews</mark> on small chunks, so that reviewers do not lose concentration during an individual <mark>review</mark> and/or the <mark>review</mark> meeting (when held)
Providing feedback from <mark>reviews</mark> to stakeholders and authors so they can improve the product and their activities (see section 3.2.1)
Providing adequate time to participants to prepare for the <mark>review</mark>
Support from management for the <mark>review</mark> process
Making <mark>reviews</mark> part of the organization’s culture, to promote learning and process improvement

techcat.statement: Distinguish <mark>black-box test techniques</mark>, <mark>white-box test techniques</mark> and <mark>experience-based</mark>

excerpt.html: <mark>Test techniques</mark> support the tester in test analysis (what to test) and in test design (how to test). … <mark>Test techniques</mark> help to develop a relatively small, but sufficient, set of <mark>test cases</mark> in a systematic way. … <mark>Test techniques</mark> also help the tester to define test conditions, identify <mark>coverage items</mark>, and identify test data during the test analysis and design. … Further information on <mark>test techniques</mark> can be found in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-4 standard, and in (Beizer 1990, Craig 2002, Copeland 2004, Koomen 2006, Jorgensen 2014, Ammann 2016, Forgács 2019). … In this syllabus, <mark>test techniques</mark> are classified as <mark>black-box</mark>, <mark>white-box</mark>, and <mark>experience-based</mark>. … <mark>Black-box test techniques</mark> (also known as specification-based techniques) are based on an analysis of the specified behavior of the <mark>test object</mark> without reference to its internal structure. … Therefore, the <mark>test cases</mark> are independent of how the software is implemented. … Consequently, if the implementation changes, but the required behavior stays the same, then the <mark>test cases</mark> are still useful. … <mark>White-box test techniques</mark> (also known as structure-based techniques) are based on an analysis of the <mark>test object</mark>’s internal structure and processing. … As the <mark>test cases</mark> are dependent on how the software is designed, they can only be created after the design or implementation of the <mark>test object</mark>. … <mark>Experience-based test techniques</mark> effectively use the knowledge and experience of testers for the design and implementation of <mark>test cases</mark>. … The effectiveness of these <mark>test techniques</mark> depends heavily on the tester’s skills. … <mark>Experience-based test techniques</mark> can detect <mark>defects</mark> that may be missed using the <mark>black-box test techniques</mark> and <mark>white-box test techniques</mark>. … Hence, <mark>experience-based test techniques</mark> are complementary to the <mark>black-box test techniques</mark> and <mark>white-box test techniques</mark>.

<mark>Equivalence Partitioning</mark> (EP) divides data into partitions (known as <mark>equivalence</mark> partitions) based on the expectation that all the elements of a given partition are to be processed in the same way by the test object. … The theory behind this technique is that if a <mark>test case</mark>, that tests one value from an <mark>equivalence</mark> partition, detects a defect, this defect should also be detected by <mark>test cases</mark> that test any other value from the same partition. … <mark>Equivalence</mark> partitions can be identified for any data element related to the test object, including inputs, outputs, configuration items, internal values, time-related values, and interface parameters. …

… Therefore, <mark>partitioning</mark> should be done with care. … In EP, the <mark>coverage</mark> items are the <mark>equivalence</mark> partitions. … To achieve 100% <mark>coverage</mark> with this test technique, <mark>test cases</mark> must exercise all identified partitions (including invalid partitions) by covering each partition at least once. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of partitions exercised by at least one <mark>test case</mark>, divided by the total number of identified partitions, and is expressed as a percentage. … Many test items include multiple sets of partitions (e.g., test items with more than one input parameter), which means that a <mark>test case</mark> will cover partitions from different sets of partitions. … The simplest <mark>coverage</mark> criterion in the case of multiple sets of partitions is called <mark>Each Choice</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> (Ammann 2016). … <mark>Each Choice</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> requires <mark>test cases</mark> to exercise each partition from each set of partitions at least once. … <mark>Each Choice</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> does not take into account combinations of partitions.

bva.statement: Use <mark>boundary value analysis</mark> to derive test cases

excerpt.html: <mark>Boundary Value Analysis</mark> (BVA) is a test technique based on exercising the boundaries of equivalence partitions. … The minimum and maximum values of a partition are its <mark>boundary</mark> values. … BVA focuses on the <mark>boundary</mark> values of the partitions because developers are more likely to make errors with these <mark>boundary</mark> values. … They differ in terms of <mark>coverage</mark> items per <mark>boundary</mark> that need to be exercised to achieve 100% <mark>coverage</mark>. … In 2-value BVA (Craig 2002, Myers 2011), for each <mark>boundary</mark> value there are two <mark>coverage</mark> items: this <mark>boundary</mark> value and its closest neighbor belonging to the adjacent partition. … To achieve 100% <mark>coverage</mark> with 2-value BVA, test cases must exercise all <mark>coverage</mark> items, i.e., all identified <mark>boundary</mark> values. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of <mark>boundary</mark> values that were exercised, divided by the total number of identified <mark>boundary</mark> values, and is expressed as a percentage. … In 3-value BVA (Koomen 2006, O’Regan 2019), for each <mark>boundary</mark> value there are three <mark>coverage</mark> items: this <mark>boundary</mark> value and both its neighbors. … Therefore, in 3-value BVA some of the <mark>coverage</mark> items may not be <mark>boundary</mark> values. … To achieve 100% <mark>coverage</mark> with 3-value BVA, test cases must exercise all <mark>coverage</mark> items, i.e., identified <mark>boundary</mark> values and their neighbors. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of <mark>boundary</mark> values and their neighbors exercised, divided by the total number of identified <mark>boundary</mark> values and their neighbors, and is expressed as a percentage. …

dt.statement: Use <mark>decision table</mark> testing to derive test cases

excerpt.html: <mark>Decision tables</mark> are used for testing the implementation of requirements that specify how different combinations of conditions result in different outcomes. … <mark>Decision tables</mark> are an effective way of recording complex logic, such as business rules. … When creating <mark>decision tables</mark>, the conditions and the resulting actions of the system are defined. … Each column corresponds to a <mark>decision</mark> rule that defines a unique combination of conditions, along with the associated actions. … In limited-entry <mark>decision tables</mark> all the values of the conditions and actions (except for irrelevant or infeasible ones; see below) are shown as Boolean values (true or false). … Alternatively, in extended-entry <mark>decision tables</mark> some or all the conditions and actions may also take on multiple values (e.g., ranges of numbers, equivalence partitions, discrete values). … A full <mark>decision table</mark> has enough columns to cover every combination of conditions. … <mark>Decision table</mark> minimization algorithms are out of scope of this syllabus. … In <mark>decision table</mark> testing, the <mark>coverage</mark> items are the columns containing feasible combinations of conditions. … To achieve 100% <mark>coverage</mark> with this technique, test cases must exercise all these columns. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of exercised columns, divided by the total number of feasible columns, and is expressed as a percentage. … The strength of <mark>decision table</mark> testing is that it provides a systematic approach to identify all the combinations of conditions, some of which might otherwise be overlooked. … It also helps to find any gaps or <mark>contradictions</mark> in the requirements. … If there are many conditions, exercising all the <mark>decision</mark> rules may be time consuming, since the number of rules grows exponentially with the number of conditions. … In such a case, to reduce the number of rules that need to be exercised, a minimized <mark>decision table</mark> or a riskbased approach may be used.

A <mark>state</mark> diagram models the behavior of a system by showing its possible <mark>states</mark> and valid <mark>state</mark> <mark>transitions</mark>. … A <mark>transition</mark> is initiated by an event, which may be additionally qualified by a guard condition. … The <mark>transitions</mark> are assumed to be instantaneous and may sometimes result in the software taking action. … The common <mark>transition</mark> labeling syntax is as follows: “event [guard condition] / action”. … A <mark>state</mark> table is a model equivalent to a <mark>state</mark> diagram. … Its rows represent <mark>states</mark>, and its columns represent events (together with guard conditions if they exist). … Table entries (cells) represent <mark>transitions</mark>, and contain the target <mark>state</mark>, as well as the resulting actions, if defined. … In contrast to the <mark>state</mark> diagram, the <mark>state</mark> table explicitly shows invalid <mark>transitions</mark>, which are represented by empty cells. … A <mark>test case</mark> based on a <mark>state</mark> diagram or <mark>state</mark> table is usually represented as a sequence of events, which results in a sequence of <mark>state</mark> changes (and actions, if needed). … One <mark>test case</mark> may, and usually will, cover several <mark>transitions</mark> between <mark>states</mark>. … There exist many <mark>coverage</mark> criteria for <mark>state</mark> <mark>transition</mark> testing. …

In <mark>all states</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>, the <mark>coverage</mark> items are the <mark>states</mark>. … To achieve 100% <mark>all states</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>, <mark>test cases</mark> must ensure that all the <mark>states</mark> are exercised. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of exercised <mark>states</mark> divided by the total number of <mark>states</mark> and is expressed as a percentage. … In valid <mark>transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> (also called 0-switch <mark>coverage</mark>), the <mark>coverage</mark> items are single valid <mark>transitions</mark>. … To achieve 100% valid <mark>transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>, <mark>test cases</mark> must exercise all the valid <mark>transitions</mark>. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of exercised valid <mark>transitions</mark> divided by the total number of valid <mark>transitions</mark> and is expressed as a percentage. … In <mark>all transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>, the <mark>coverage</mark> items are all the <mark>transitions</mark> shown in a <mark>state</mark> table. … To achieve 100% <mark>all transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>, <mark>test cases</mark> must exercise all the valid <mark>transitions</mark> and attempt to execute invalid <mark>transitions</mark>. … Testing only one invalid <mark>transition</mark> in a single <mark>test case</mark> helps to avoid defect masking, i.e., a situation in which one defect prevents the detection of another. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of valid and invalid <mark>transitions</mark> exercised or attempted to be covered by executed <mark>test cases</mark>, divided by the total number of valid and invalid <mark>transitions</mark>, and is expressed as a percentage. … <mark>All states</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> is weaker than valid <mark>transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>, because it can typically be achieved without exercising all the <mark>transitions</mark>. … Valid <mark>transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> is the most widely used <mark>coverage</mark> criterion. … Achieving full valid <mark>transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> guarantees full <mark>all states</mark> <mark>coverage</mark>. … Achieving full <mark>all transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> guarantees both full <mark>all states</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> and full valid <mark>transitions</mark> <mark>coverage</mark> and should be a minimum requirement for mission and <mark>safety-critical</mark> software.

In <mark>statement</mark> testing, the <mark>coverage</mark> items are executable <mark>statements</mark>. … The aim is to design test cases that exercise <mark>statements</mark> in the code until an acceptable level of <mark>coverage</mark> is achieved. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of <mark>statements</mark> exercised by the test cases divided by the total number of executable <mark>statements</mark> in the code, and is expressed as a percentage. … When 100% <mark>statement coverage</mark> is achieved, it ensures that all executable <mark>statements</mark> in the code have been exercised at least once. … In particular, this means that each <mark>statement</mark> with a <mark>defect</mark> will be executed, which may cause a failure demonstrating the presence of the <mark>defect</mark>. … However, exercising a <mark>statement</mark> with a test case will not detect <mark>defects</mark> in all cases. … For example, it may not detect <mark>defects</mark> that are data dependent (e.g., a division by zero that only fails when a denominator is set to zero). … Also, 100% <mark>statement coverage</mark> does not ensure that all the decision logic has been tested as, for instance, it may not exercise all the <mark>branches</mark> (see chapter 4.3.2) in the code.

A <mark>branch</mark> is a transfer of control between two nodes in the control flow graph, which shows the possible sequences in which source code <mark>statements</mark> are executed in the test object. … In <mark>branch</mark> testing the <mark>coverage</mark> items are <mark>branches</mark> and the aim is to design test cases to exercise <mark>branches</mark> in the code until an acceptable level of <mark>coverage</mark> is achieved. … <mark>Coverage</mark> is measured as the number of <mark>branches</mark> exercised by the test cases divided by the total number of <mark>branches</mark> and is expressed as a percentage. … When 100% <mark>branch coverage</mark> is achieved, all <mark>branches</mark> in the code, unconditional and conditional, are exercised by test cases. … Conditional <mark>branches</mark> typically correspond to a true or false outcome from an “if...then” decision, an outcome from a switch/case <mark>statement</mark>, or a decision to exit or continue in a loop. … However, exercising a <mark>branch</mark> with a test case will not detect <mark>defects</mark> in all cases. … For example, it may not detect <mark>defects</mark> requiring the execution of a specific path in a code. … <mark>Branch coverage</mark> subsumes <mark>statement coverage</mark>. … This means that any set of test cases achieving 100% <mark>branch coverage</mark> also achieves 100% <mark>statement coverage</mark> (but not vice versa).

whitebox.statement: Explain the value of white-box testing

excerpt.html: A fundamental strength that all white-box test techniques share is that the entire software implementation is taken into account during testing, which facilitates <mark>defect</mark> detection even when the software specification is vague, outdated or incomplete. … A corresponding weakness is that if the software does not implement one or more requirements, white-box testing may not detect the resulting <mark>defects</mark> of omission (Watson 1996). … Performing only black-box testing does not provide a measure of actual code <mark>coverage</mark>. … White-box <mark>coverage</mark> measures provide an objective measurement of <mark>coverage</mark> and the necessary information to allow additional tests to be generated to increase this <mark>coverage</mark>, and subsequently increase confidence in the code.
<mark>Error guessing</mark> is a test technique used to anticipate the occurrence of <mark>errors</mark>, <mark>defects</mark>, and failures, based on the tester’s knowledge, including:
The types of <mark>errors</mark> the developers tend to make and the types of <mark>defects</mark> that result from these <mark>errors</mark>

In general, <mark>errors</mark>, <mark>defects</mark> and failures may be related to: input (e.g., correct input not accepted, parameters wrong or missing), output (e.g., wrong format, wrong result), logic (e.g., missing cases, wrong operator), computation (e.g., incorrect operand, wrong computation), interfaces (e.g., parameter mismatch, incompatible types), or data (e.g., incorrect initialization, wrong type). … Fault attacks are a way to implement <mark>error guessing</mark>. … This test technique requires the tester to create or acquire a list of possible <mark>errors</mark>, <mark>defects</mark> and failures, and to design tests that will identify <mark>defects</mark> associated with the <mark>errors</mark>, expose the <mark>defects</mark>, or cause the failures. … These lists can be built based on experience, <mark>defect</mark> and failure data, or from common knowledge about why software fails. … See (Whittaker 2002, Whittaker 2003, Andrews 2006) for more information on <mark>error guessing</mark> and fault attacks.

In <mark>exploratory testing</mark>, tests are simultaneously designed, executed, and evaluated while the tester learns about the test object. … <mark>Exploratory testing</mark> is sometimes performed using session-based testing to structure the testing. … In a session-based approach, <mark>exploratory testing</mark> is performed within a defined time box. … The tester uses a <mark>test charter</mark> containing test objectives to guide the testing. … <mark>Coverage</mark> items are identified and exercised during the test session. … <mark>Exploratory testing</mark> is useful when there are few or inadequate specifications or there is significant time pressure on the testing. … <mark>Exploratory testing</mark> is also useful to complement other more formal test techniques. … <mark>Exploratory testing</mark> will be more effective if the tester is experienced, has domain knowledge and has a high degree of essential skills, like analytical skills, curiosity and creativeness (see section 1.5.1). … <mark>Exploratory testing</mark> can incorporate the use of other test techniques (e.g., <mark>equivalence partitioning</mark>). … More information about <mark>exploratory testing</mark> can be found in (Kaner 1999, Whittaker 2009, Hendrickson 2013).

In <mark>checklist-based testing</mark>, a tester designs, implements, and executes tests to cover test conditions from a <mark>checklist</mark>. … <mark>Checklists</mark> can be built based on experience, knowledge about what is important for the user, or an understanding of why and how software fails. … <mark>Checklists</mark> should not contain items that can be checked automatically, items better suited as entry criteria, exit criteria, or items that are too general (Brykczynski 1999).

<mark>Checklist</mark> items are often phrased in the form of a question. … <mark>Checklists</mark> can be created to support various test types, including functional and non-functional testing (e.g., 10 heuristics for usability testing (Nielsen 1994)). … Some <mark>checklist</mark> entries may gradually become less effective over time because the developers will learn to avoid making the same <mark>errors</mark>. … New entries may also need to be added to reflect newly found high severity <mark>defects</mark>. … Therefore, <mark>checklists</mark> should be regularly updated based on <mark>defect</mark> analysis. … However, care should be taken to avoid letting the <mark>checklist</mark> become too long (Gawande 2009). … In the absence of detailed <mark>test cases</mark>, <mark>checklist-based testing</mark> can provide guidelines and some degree of consistency for the testing. … If the <mark>checklists</mark> are high-level, some variability in the actual testing is likely to occur, resulting in potentially greater <mark>coverage</mark> but less repeatability.

atdd.statement: Explain how to write user stories in collaboration with developers and business

excerpt.html: A user story represents a feature that will be valuable to either a user or purchaser of a system or software. User stories have three critical aspects (Jeffries 2000), called together the “3 C’s”:
Confirmation – the <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> (see section 4.5.2)

The most common format for a user story is “As a [role], I want [goal to be accomplished], so that I can [resulting business value for the role]”, followed by the <mark>acceptance criteria</mark>. … Good user stories should be: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable (<mark>INVEST</mark>). …

atdd.statement: Classify the different options for writing <mark>acceptance criteria</mark>

excerpt.html: <mark>Acceptance criteria</mark> for a user story are the conditions that an implementation of the user story must meet to be accepted by stakeholders. … From this perspective, <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> may be viewed as the test conditions that should be exercised by the tests. … <mark>Acceptance criteria</mark> are usually a result of the Conversation (see section 4.5.1). … <mark>Acceptance criteria</mark> are used to:
There are several ways to write <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> for a user story. …

Most <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> can be documented in one of these two formats. … However, the team may use another, custom format, as long as the <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> are well-defined and unambiguous.

atdd.statement: Use acceptance test-driven development (ATDD) to derive <mark>test cases</mark>

excerpt.html: … <mark>Test cases</mark> are created prior to implementing the user story. … The <mark>test cases</mark> are created by team members with different perspectives, e.g., customers, developers, and testers (Adzic 2009). … <mark>Test cases</mark> may be executed manually or automated. … The first step is a specification <mark>workshop</mark> where the user story and (if not yet defined) its <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> are analyzed, discussed, and written by the team members. … The next step is to create the <mark>test cases</mark>. … The <mark>test cases</mark> are based on the <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> and can be seen as examples of how the software works. … Typically, the first <mark>test cases</mark> are positive, confirming the correct behavior without exceptions or error conditions, and comprising the sequence of activities executed if everything goes as expected. … After the positive <mark>test cases</mark> are done, the team should perform negative testing. … <mark>Test cases</mark> should be expressed in a way that is understandable for the stakeholders. … Typically, <mark>test cases</mark> contain sentences in natural language involving the necessary preconditions (if any), the inputs, and the postconditions. … The <mark>test cases</mark> must cover all the characteristics of the user story and should not go beyond the story. … However, the <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> may detail some of the issues described in the user story. … In addition, no two <mark>test cases</mark> should describe the same characteristics of the user story. … When captured in a format supported by a test automation framework, the developers can automate the <mark>test cases</mark> by writing the supporting code as they implement the feature described by a user story. …

plan.statement: Exemplify the purpose and content of a <mark>test plan</mark>
plan.section: 5.1.1 Purpose and Content of a Test Plan

excerpt.html: A <mark>test plan</mark> describes the <mark>test objectives</mark>, resources and processes for a test project. … A <mark>test plan</mark>:
Documents the means and schedule for achieving <mark>test objectives</mark>
Demonstrates that testing will adhere to the existing test policy and <mark>test strategy</mark> (or explains why the testing will deviate from them)

Test planning guides the testers’ thinking and forces the testers to confront the future challenges related to <mark>risks</mark>, schedules, people, tools, costs, effort, etc. … The process of preparing a <mark>test plan</mark> is a useful way to think through the efforts needed to achieve the <mark>test objectives</mark>. … The typical content of a <mark>test plan</mark> includes:
Context of testing (e.g., test scope, <mark>test objectives</mark>, <mark>test basis</mark>)
<mark>Risk</mark> register (e.g., <mark>product risks</mark>, <mark>project risks</mark>)

<mark>Test approach</mark> (e.g., <mark>test levels</mark>, <mark>test types</mark>, <mark>test techniques</mark>, test deliverables, <mark>entry</mark> criteria and <mark>exit criteria</mark>, independence of testing, metrics to be collected, <mark>test data</mark> requirements, test environment requirements, deviations from the test policy and <mark>test strategy</mark>)
More details about the <mark>test plan</mark> and its content can be found in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 standard.

plan.statement: Compare and contrast <mark>entry</mark> criteria and <mark>exit criteria</mark>

excerpt.html: <mark>Entry</mark> criteria define the preconditions for undertaking a given activity. … If <mark>entry</mark> criteria are not met, it is likely that the activity will prove to be more difficult, time-consuming, costly, and riskier. … <mark>Exit criteria</mark> define what must be achieved to declare an activity completed. … <mark>Entry</mark> criteria and <mark>exit criteria</mark> should be defined for each <mark>test level</mark>, and will differ based on the <mark>test objectives</mark>. … Typical <mark>entry</mark> criteria include: availability of resources (e.g., people, tools, environments, <mark>test data</mark>, budget, time), availability of <mark>testware</mark> (e.g., <mark>test basis</mark>, testable requirements, user stories, test cases), and initial quality level of a <mark>test object</mark> (e.g., all smoke tests have passed). … Typical <mark>exit criteria</mark> include: measures of thoroughness (e.g., achieved level of <mark>coverage</mark>, number of unresolved <mark>defects</mark>, <mark>defect</mark> density, number of failed test cases), and binary “yes/no” criteria (e.g., planned tests have been executed, static testing has been performed, all <mark>defects</mark> found are reported, all regression tests are automated). … Running out of time or budget can also be viewed as valid <mark>exit criteria</mark>. … Even without other <mark>exit criteria</mark> being satisfied, it can be acceptable to end testing under such circumstances, if the stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the <mark>risk</mark> to go live without further testing. … In Agile software development, <mark>exit criteria</mark> are often called Definition of Done, defining the team’s objective metrics for a releasable item. … <mark>Entry</mark> criteria that a <mark>user story</mark> must fulfill to start the development and/or testing activities are called Definition of Ready.

relplan.statement: Recognize how a tester adds value to <mark>iteration</mark> and <mark>release planning</mark>
relplan.section: 5.1.2 Tester's Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning
keywords: break down user stories into tasks
detailed risk analysis of user stories
determine the testability of user stories
plan the testing for the release

excerpt.html: In iterative SDLCs, typically two kinds of <mark>planning</mark> occur: <mark>release planning</mark> and <mark>iteration planning</mark>. … <mark>Release planning</mark> looks ahead to the <mark>release</mark> of a product, defines and re-defines the <mark>product backlog</mark>, and may involve refining larger user stories into a set of smaller user stories. … It also serves as the basis for the <mark>test approach</mark> and <mark>test plan</mark> across all <mark>iterations</mark>. … Testers involved in <mark>release planning</mark> participate in writing testable user stories and <mark>acceptance criteria</mark> (see section 4.5), participate in <mark>project and quality risk analyses</mark> (see section 5.2), estimate test effort associated with user stories (see section 5.1.4), <mark>determine the test approach</mark>, and <mark>plan the testing for the release</mark>. … <mark>Iteration planning</mark> looks ahead to the end of a single <mark>iteration</mark> and is concerned with the <mark>iteration backlog</mark>. … Testers involved in <mark>iteration planning</mark> participate in the <mark>detailed risk analysis of user stories</mark>, <mark>determine the testability of user stories</mark>, <mark>break down user stories into tasks</mark> (<mark>particularly testing tasks</mark>), estimate test effort for all testing tasks, and identify and refine functional and non-functional aspects of the <mark>test object</mark>.

estimate.statement: Use <mark>estimation</mark> techniques to calculate the required test effort

excerpt.html: Test effort <mark>estimation</mark> involves predicting the amount of test-related work needed to meet the test objectives of a test project. … It is important to make it clear to the stakeholders that the estimate is based on a number of assumptions and is always subject to <mark>estimation</mark> error. … <mark>Estimation</mark> for small tasks is usually more accurate than for the large ones. … In this syllabus, the following four <mark>estimation</mark> techniques are described. … <mark>Estimation</mark> based on ratios. … The ratios of an organization’s own projects (e.g., taken from historical data) are generally the best source to use in the <mark>estimation</mark> process. …

… In this iterative, expert-based technique, experts make experience-based <mark>estimations</mark>. … Each expert is then asked to make a new <mark>estimation</mark> based on that feedback, again in isolation. … Three-point <mark>estimation</mark>. … In this expert-based technique, three <mark>estimations</mark> are made by the experts: the most optimistic <mark>estimation</mark> (a), the most likely <mark>estimation</mark> (m) and the most pessimistic <mark>estimation</mark> (b). … For example, if the estimates (in personhours) are: a=6, m=9 and b=18, then the final <mark>estimation</mark> is 10±2 person-hours (i.e., between 8 and 12 person-hours), because E = (6 + 4*9 + 18) / 6 = 10 and SD = (18 – 6) / 6 = 2. … See (Kan 2003, Koomen 2006, Westfall 2009) for these and many other test <mark>estimation</mark> techniques.

Once the <mark>test cases</mark> and test procedures are specified and assembled into test suites, these test suites can be arranged in a <mark>test execution schedule</mark> that defines the order in which they are to be run. … When prioritizing <mark>test cases</mark>, different factors can be taken into account. … The most commonly used <mark>test case</mark> <mark>prioritization</mark> strategies are as follows:

<mark>Risk-based</mark> <mark>prioritization</mark>, where the order of <mark>test execution</mark> is based on the results of risk analysis (see section 5.2.3). <mark>Test cases</mark> covering the most important risks are executed first.

<mark>Coverage-based</mark> <mark>prioritization</mark>, where the order of <mark>test execution</mark> is based on <mark>coverage</mark> (e.g., statement <mark>coverage</mark>). <mark>Test cases</mark> achieving the highest <mark>coverage</mark> are executed first. In another variant, called additional <mark>coverage</mark> <mark>prioritization</mark>, the <mark>test case</mark> achieving the highest <mark>coverage</mark> is executed first; each subsequent <mark>test case</mark> is the one that achieves the highest additional <mark>coverage</mark>.

<mark>Requirements-based</mark> <mark>prioritization</mark>, where the order of <mark>test execution</mark> is based on the priorities of the requirements traced back to the corresponding <mark>test cases</mark>. Requirement priorities are defined by stakeholders. <mark>Test cases</mark> related to the most important requirements are executed first.

Ideally, <mark>test cases</mark> would be ordered to run based on their priority levels, using, for example, one of the above-mentioned <mark>prioritization</mark> strategies. … However, this practice may not work if the <mark>test cases</mark> or the features being tested have dependencies. … If a <mark>test case</mark> with a higher priority is dependent on a <mark>test case</mark> with a lower priority, the lower priority <mark>test case</mark> must be executed first. … The order of <mark>test execution</mark> must also take into account the availability of resources. …

pyrquad.statement: Recall the concepts of the <mark>test pyramid</mark>

excerpt.html: The <mark>test pyramid</mark> is a model showing that different tests may have different granularity. … The <mark>test pyramid</mark> model supports the team in test automation and in test effort allocation by showing that different test objectives are supported by different levels of test automation. … The <mark>pyramid</mark> layers represent groups of tests. … For example, the original <mark>test pyramid</mark> model (Cohn 2009) defines three layers: “unit tests”, “service tests” and “UI tests”. … Another popular model defines unit (<mark>component</mark>) tests, integration (<mark>component</mark> integration) tests, and end-to-end tests. … Other <mark>test levels</mark> (see section 2.2.1) can also be used.

pyrquad.statement: Summarize the <mark>testing quadrants</mark> and their relationships with <mark>test levels</mark> and <mark>test types</mark>

excerpt.html: The <mark>testing quadrants</mark>, defined by Brian Marick (Marick 2003, Crispin 2008), group the <mark>test levels</mark> with the appropriate <mark>test types</mark>, activities, test techniques and work products in the Agile software development. … The model supports test management in visualizing these to ensure that all appropriate <mark>test types</mark> and <mark>test levels</mark> are included in the SDLC and in understanding that some <mark>test types</mark> are more relevant to certain <mark>test levels</mark> than others. … This model also provides a way to differentiate and describe the <mark>test types</mark> to all stakeholders, including developers, testers, and business representatives. … In this model, tests can be <mark>business facing</mark> or <mark>technology facing</mark>. … Tests can also support the team (i.e., guide the development) or <mark>critique the product</mark> (i.e., measure its behavior against the expectations). … The combination of these two viewpoints determines the four <mark>quadrants</mark>:

Quadrant Q1 (<mark>technology facing</mark>, support the team). This quadrant contains <mark>component tests</mark> and <mark>component integration tests</mark>. These tests should be automated and included in the CI process.

Quadrant Q2 (<mark>business facing</mark>, support the team). This quadrant contains <mark>functional tests</mark>, examples, <mark>user story tests</mark>, user experience prototypes, <mark>API testing</mark>, and <mark>simulations</mark>. These tests check the acceptance criteria and can be manual or automated.

Quadrant Q3 (<mark>business facing</mark>, <mark>critique the product</mark>). This quadrant contains <mark>exploratory testing</mark>, <mark>usability testing</mark>, <mark>user acceptance testing</mark>. These tests are user-oriented and often manual.

Quadrant Q4 (<mark>technology facing</mark>, <mark>critique the product</mark>). This quadrant contains <mark>smoke tests</mark> and <mark>non-functional tests</mark> (except <mark>usability</mark> tests). These tests are often automated.

risk.statement: Identify <mark>risk level</mark> by using <mark>risk</mark> likelihood and <mark>risk</mark> impact

excerpt.html: <mark>Risk</mark> is a potential event, hazard, threat, or situation whose occurrence causes an adverse effect. … A <mark>risk</mark> can be characterized by two factors:
<mark>Risk</mark> likelihood – the probability of the <mark>risk</mark> occurrence (greater than zero and less than one)
<mark>Risk</mark> impact (harm) – the consequences of this occurrence
These two factors express the <mark>risk level</mark>, which is a measure for the <mark>risk</mark>. … The higher the <mark>risk level</mark>, the more important is its treatment.
