In software testing one is generally concerned with two types of <mark>risks</mark>: <mark>project risks</mark> and <mark>product risks</mark>. … <mark>Project risks</mark> are related to the management and <mark>control</mark> of the project. … <mark>Project risks</mark> include:
<mark>Technical</mark> issues (e.g., <mark>scope creep</mark>, poor tool support)

<mark>Project risks</mark>, when they occur, may have an impact on the project schedule, budget or scope, which affects the project's ability to achieve its objectives. … <mark>Product risks</mark> are related to the product quality characteristics (e.g., described in the ISO 25010 quality model). … Examples of <mark>product risks</mark> include: missing or wrong functionality, incorrect calculations, runtime errors, poor architecture, inefficient algorithms, inadequate response time, poor user experience, security vulnerabilities. … <mark>Product risks</mark>, when they occur, may result in various negative consequences, including:

risk.statement: Explain how <mark>product risk</mark> analysis may influence thoroughness and test scope

excerpt.html: From a testing perspective, the goal of <mark>product risk</mark> analysis is to provide an awareness of <mark>product risk</mark> to focus the test effort in a way that minimizes the residual <mark>level</mark> of <mark>product risk</mark>. … Ideally, <mark>product risk</mark> analysis begins early in the SDLC. … <mark>Product risk</mark> analysis consists of <mark>risk</mark> identification and <mark>risk</mark> assessment. … <mark>Risk</mark> identification is about generating a comprehensive list of <mark>risks</mark>. … Stakeholders can identify <mark>risks</mark> by using various techniques and tools, e.g., brainstorming, workshops, interviews, or cause-effect diagrams. … <mark>Risk</mark> assessment involves: categorization of identified <mark>risks</mark>, determining their <mark>risk</mark> likelihood, <mark>risk</mark> impact and <mark>risk level</mark>, prioritizing, and proposing ways to handle them. … Categorization helps in assigning mitigation actions, because usually <mark>risks</mark> falling into the same category can be mitigated using a similar approach. … <mark>Risk</mark> assessment can use a quantitative or qualitative approach, or a mix of them. … In the quantitative approach the <mark>risk level</mark> is calculated as the multiplication of <mark>risk</mark> likelihood and <mark>risk</mark> impact. … In the qualitative approach the <mark>risk level</mark> can be determined using a <mark>risk</mark> matrix. … <mark>Product risk</mark> analysis may influence the thoroughness and test scope. …
Determine the particular test <mark>levels</mark> and propose test types to be performed
Determine whether any activities in addition to testing could be employed to reduce <mark>risk</mark>

risk.statement: Explain what measures can be taken in response to analyzed <mark>product risks</mark>

excerpt.html: <mark>Product risk</mark> control comprises all measures that are taken in response to identified and assessed <mark>product risks</mark>. … <mark>Product risk</mark> control consists of <mark>risk</mark> mitigation and <mark>risk</mark> monitoring. … <mark>Risk</mark> mitigation involves implementing the actions proposed in <mark>risk</mark> assessment to reduce the <mark>risk level</mark>. … The aim of <mark>risk</mark> monitoring is to ensure that the mitigation actions are effective, to obtain further information to improve <mark>risk</mark> assessment, and to identify emerging <mark>risks</mark>. … With respect to <mark>product risk</mark> control, once a <mark>risk</mark> has been analyzed, several response options to <mark>risk</mark> are possible, e.g., <mark>risk</mark> mitigation by testing, <mark>risk</mark> acceptance, <mark>risk</mark> transfer, or a contingency plan (Veenendaal 2012). … Actions that can be taken to mitigate the <mark>product risks</mark> by testing are as follows:
Select the testers with the right <mark>level</mark> of experience and skills, suitable for a given <mark>risk</mark> type
Apply an appropriate <mark>level</mark> of independence of testing
Perform <mark>reviews</mark> and static <mark>analysis</mark>
Apply the appropriate test techniques and coverage <mark>levels</mark>

In testing, <mark>configuration</mark> management (CM) provides a discipline for identifying, controlling, and tracking work products such as <mark>test plans</mark>, test strategies, test conditions, <mark>test cases</mark>, test scripts, test results, test logs, and test reports as <mark>configuration</mark> items. … For a complex <mark>configuration</mark> item (e.g., a test environment), CM records the items it consists of, their relationships, and <mark>versions</mark>. … If the <mark>configuration</mark> item is approved for testing, it becomes a baseline and can only be changed through a formal change control process. … <mark>Configuration</mark> management keeps a record of changed <mark>configuration</mark> items when a new baseline is created. …

All <mark>configuration</mark> items, including test items (individual parts of the test object), are uniquely identified, <mark>version</mark> controlled, tracked for changes, and related to other <mark>configuration</mark> items so that traceability can be maintained throughout the test process
All identified documentation and software items are referenced unambiguously in <mark>testware</mark>

Since one of the major test objectives is to find <mark>defects</mark>, an established <mark>defect management</mark> process is essential. … Although we refer to "<mark>defects</mark>" here, the reported anomalies may turn out to be real <mark>defects</mark> or something else (e.g., false–positive result, change request) - this is resolved during the process of dealing with the <mark>defect</mark> reports. … At a minimum, the <mark>defect management</mark> process includes a workflow for handling individual <mark>defects</mark> or anomalies from their discovery to their closure and rules for their classification. … The workflow typically comprises activities to log the reported anomalies, analyze and classify them, decide on a suitable response such as to fix or keep it as it is and finally to close the <mark>defect</mark> report. … It is advisable to handle <mark>defects</mark> from static testing (especially static analysis) in a similar way. … Typical <mark>defect</mark> reports have the following objectives:
Provide those responsible for handling and resolving reported <mark>defects</mark> with sufficient information to resolve the issue
A <mark>defect</mark> report logged during dynamic testing typically includes:

Context of the <mark>defect</mark> (e.g., <mark>test case</mark> being run, test activity being performed, SDLC phase, and other relevant information such as the test technique, checklist or test data being used)
Severity of the <mark>defect</mark> (degree of impact) on the interests of stakeholders or requirements
Status of the <mark>defect</mark> (e.g., open, deferred, duplicate, waiting to be fixed, awaiting confirmation testing, re-opened, closed, rejected)
References (e.g., to the <mark>test case</mark>)

Some of this data may be automatically included when using <mark>defect management</mark> tools (e.g., identifier, date, author and initial status). … Document templates for a <mark>defect</mark> report and example <mark>defect</mark> reports can be found in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 standard, which refers to <mark>defect</mark> reports as incident reports.

Since one of the major test objectives is to find <mark>defects</mark>, an established <mark>defect</mark> management process is essential. … Although we refer to "<mark>defects</mark>" here, the reported anomalies may turn out to be real <mark>defects</mark> or something else (e.g., false–positive result, change request) - this is resolved during the process of dealing with the <mark>defect reports</mark>. … At a minimum, the <mark>defect</mark> management process includes a workflow for handling individual <mark>defects</mark> or anomalies from their discovery to their closure and rules for their classification. … The workflow typically comprises activities to log the reported anomalies, analyze and classify them, decide on a suitable response such as to fix or keep it as it is and finally to close the <mark>defect report</mark>. … It is advisable to handle <mark>defects</mark> from static testing (especially static analysis) in a similar way. … Typical <mark>defect reports</mark> have the following objectives:
Provide those responsible for handling and resolving reported <mark>defects</mark> with sufficient information to resolve the issue
A <mark>defect report</mark> logged during dynamic testing typically includes:
Identification of the <mark>test object</mark> and test environment
Context of the <mark>defect</mark> (e.g., test case being run, test activity being performed, SDLC phase, and other relevant information such as the test technique, checklist or test data being used)

Description of the <mark>failure</mark> to enable reproduction and resolution including the test steps that detected the anomaly, and any relevant test logs, database dumps, screenshots, or recordings
<mark>Severity</mark> of the <mark>defect</mark> (degree of impact) on the interests of stakeholders or requirements
<mark>Priority to fix</mark>
Status of the <mark>defect</mark> (e.g., open, deferred, duplicate, waiting to be fixed, awaiting confirmation testing, re-opened, closed, rejected)

<mark>Test metrics</mark> are gathered to show <mark>progress</mark> against the planned test schedule and budget, the current quality of the test object, and the effectiveness of the test activities with respect to the test objectives or an iteration goal. … Test monitoring gathers a variety of metrics to support the test control and <mark>test completion</mark>. … Common <mark>test metrics</mark> include:
Project <mark>progress</mark> metrics (e.g., task <mark>completion</mark>, resource usage, test <mark>effort</mark>)

Test <mark>progress</mark> metrics (e.g., test case implementation <mark>progress</mark>, test environment preparation <mark>progress</mark>, number of test cases run/not run, passed/failed, test execution time)
<mark>Defect</mark> metrics (e.g., number and priorities of <mark>defects</mark> found/fixed, <mark>defect</mark> density, <mark>defect</mark> detection percentage)
<mark>Risk</mark> metrics (e.g., residual <mark>risk</mark> level)

reports.statement: Summarize the purposes, content, and audiences for test <mark>reports</mark>
reports.section: 5.3.2 Purpose, Content and Audience for Test Reports

excerpt.html: … <mark>Test progress reports</mark> support the ongoing test control and must provide enough information to make modifications to the test schedule, resources, or <mark>test plan</mark>, when such changes are needed due to deviation from the plan or changed circumstances. … <mark>Test completion reports</mark> summarize a specific test activity (e.g., <mark>test level</mark>, test cycle, iteration) and can give information for subsequent testing. … During test monitoring and test control, the test team generates <mark>test progress reports</mark> for stakeholders to keep them informed. … <mark>Test progress reports</mark> are usually generated on a regular basis (e.g., daily, weekly, etc.) and include:
Test <mark>progress</mark> (e.g., ahead or behind schedule), including any notable deviations
<mark>Impediments</mark> for testing, and their <mark>workarounds</mark>
<mark>Test metrics</mark> (see section 5.3.1 for examples)
New and changed <mark>risks</mark> within testing period

A <mark>test completion report</mark> is prepared during <mark>test completion</mark>, when a project, <mark>test level</mark>, or test type is complete and when, ideally, its <mark>exit criteria</mark> have been met. … This <mark>report</mark> uses <mark>test progress reports</mark> and other data. … Typical <mark>test completion reports</mark> include:
<mark>Test summary</mark>
Testing and product quality evaluation based on the original <mark>test plan</mark> (i.e., test objectives and <mark>exit criteria</mark>)
Deviations from the <mark>test plan</mark> (e.g., differences from the planned test schedule, duration, and <mark>effort</mark>).

tooltypes.statement: Explain how different types of test tools support testing
keywords: difficult or impossible to perform manually
tools supporting scalability and deployment standardization

excerpt.html: Test tools support and facilitate many test activities. Examples include, but are not limited to:
Test <mark>management tools</mark> – increase the <mark>test process</mark> efficiency by facilitating management of the SDLC, requirements, tests, <mark>defects</mark>, configuration
<mark>Static testing</mark> tools – support the tester in performing <mark>reviews</mark> and <mark>static analysis</mark>
<mark>Test design</mark> and <mark>test implementation</mark> tools – facilitate generation of <mark>test cases</mark>, <mark>test data</mark> and <mark>test procedures</mark>
<mark>Test execution</mark> and test <mark>coverage</mark> tools – facilitate <mark>automated test execution</mark> and <mark>coverage measurement</mark>
<mark>Non-functional testing</mark> tools – allow the tester to perform <mark>non-functional testing</mark> that is <mark>difficult or impossible to perform manually</mark>
<mark>DevOps tools</mark> – support the DevOps <mark>delivery pipeline</mark>, <mark>workflow tracking</mark>, <mark>automated build</mark> process(es), CI/CD
Collaboration tools – <mark>facilitate communication</mark>
<mark>Tools supporting scalability and deployment standardization</mark> (e.g., <mark>virtual machines</mark>, <mark>containerization tools</mark>)

automation.statement: Recall the benefits and <mark>risks</mark> of <mark>test automation</mark>
automation.section: 6.2 Benefits and Risks of Test Automation

excerpt.html: … There are also some <mark>risks</mark>, which need analysis and mitigation. … Potential benefits of using <mark>test automation</mark> include:
More objective assessment (e.g., <mark>coverage</mark>) and providing measures that are too complicated for humans to determine
Reduced test execution times to provide earlier <mark>defect</mark> detection, faster feedback and faster time to market
Potential <mark>risks</mark> of using <mark>test automation</mark> include:

The dependency on the tool vendor which may go out of business, retire the tool, sell the tool to a different vendor or provide poor support (e.g., responses to queries, upgrades, and <mark>defect</mark> fixes).
The <mark>automation</mark> tool is not compatible with the development platform.
